title: Access Token Manipulation
summary: Access token manipulation abuses the Windows object that carries a process identity and its group memberships. Every process runs with an access token, and that token decides which files, registry keys and services the process may touch. An attacker who already holds administrator rights can duplicate a token from another process, create a fresh token from known credentials, or edit directory attributes that are folded into a token, then attach the result to a running thread or to a brand new process. The consequence is that actions appear to come from a different account, frequently the SYSTEM account, so file and network access succeeds without the attacker ever holding that account password. Telemetry shows the gap between the account that started a process and the account the process actually uses: process creation events whose user field does not match the interactive session, logon events of type 9 for a new credential material, unusual process lineage, and remote authentication from an account that never logged on locally. Legitimate system behaviour shares some of this shape, because Windows itself uses these interfaces for User Account Control and services, so defenders baseline which processes normally adopt another token rather than alerting on the interfaces alone.

beginner.definition: An access token is a small digital pass that Windows gives to every running program. The pass lists who the program is acting as and what it may open. Access token manipulation means an attacker changes or copies that pass so a program acts as a more powerful user.
beginner.whyItMatters: Administrator rights on one machine are bad enough, but many systems treat the SYSTEM account as far more powerful. Attackers use copied passes to reach that level without stealing another password. The resulting activity often looks like a valid user doing valid work. Detecting it is hard unless you know how tokens behave in your own network.
howItWorks: Windows creates a pass, called an access token, when a user logs on or a service starts.
Every process started by that user or service carries a copy of the same pass.
An attacker with administrator rights takes a pass from a running process, which is called token stealing.
The stolen pass is joined to a thread, or used to start a new process, so the program inherits the rights of that other user.
Some attackers instead create a new pass from a username and password they already hold.
Other attackers edit directory information so extra rights are added to a real user pass.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel where staff use key cards instead of names. A cleaner finds a manager card left on a desk and copies its data onto a blank card. The locks cannot see a difference, so every locked room opens for the cleaner. The security desk log still shows the manager walking around all night, because the card, not the person, was checked.
takeaways: A token is the pass that decides what a program may open, so stealing one avoids stealing a password.
Watch for programs acting as an account that is not the one that started them.
Baseline which system processes normally swap tokens, because Windows also does this by design.

objectives: Explain what a Windows access token is and why it matters for permission checks.
Describe the main ways tokens can be copied, created or altered on a system.
Recognise the difference between token theft, process creation with a token and directory based injection.
Identify which log sources record logon sessions and process creation for token abuse.
Separate normal Windows token use, such as elevation prompts, from suspicious use.
